sentences.text: This creature displays two unique traits among its relatives: a fused odontoid process that lacks medial processes and a lower jaw without an external opening.
The skull is elongated, showing slight narrowing near the sockets for the fifth and eleventh upper teeth.
Its snout is flatter and less domed compared to similar genera like Sebecus and Barinasuchus.
It possessed twelve upper teeth, with blunt back teeth, a feature shared with other Paleogene sebecosuchians.
Two specific autapomorphies distinguish it: the odontoid process fuses to the axis with a vertical front surface and lacks medial projections, while the mandible lacks an external fenestra.
Similar to Lorosuchus, it features a shallow depression on the side of the infraorbital region of the jugal bone.
The jugal bone is very large and ornamented, with a rear branch higher than the front process that widens sideways, a trait previously seen only in Bretesuchus.
Like many early mesoeucrocodylian groups, it possesses a longitudinal crest running along the front of the skull.
In this species, that frontal crest is low and smooth, extending from the middle to the back of the frontal bone.
The quadratojugal bone participates in the jaw joint, creating a double connection point common to all sebecid species.
Like peirosaurids such as Hamadasuchus and Lomasuchus, it has a postdirecting bump on the squamosal bone that does not form a horn.
The tympanic cavity area contains only two openings, a condition similar to Sebecus, Hamadasuchus, and modern crocodilians.
Compared to Sebecus, the third neck vertebra has more robust and wide transverse processes, and its length is nearly equal to that of the axis.
Sahitisuchus is one of only two species formally described from the São José de Itaboraí Basin.
The species name fluminensis is a Latinization of fluminense, referring to citizens of the state of Rio de Janeiro.
The genus Sahitisuchus was named by Kellner, Pinheiro, and Campos in 2014.
The generic name honors the Xavante people, an indigenous group from Brazil.
The species is known only from a single nearly complete skull and lower jaw, along with several neck vertebrae.
The fossil was found during a five-decade exploration of the São José de Itaboraí Basin that concluded in 1984.
The holotype was briefly mentioned in 1946, 1991, and 1993 but was not formally described until 2014.
The genus Sahitisuchus was named by Alexander W. A. Kellner, André E. P. Pinheiro, and Diogenes A. Campos in 2014.
Sahitisuchus is known only from holotype MCT 1730-R, which includes an almost complete skull, mandible, proatlas, intercentrum, axis, and third vertebra.
The holotype was discovered during an exploration of the São José de Itaboraí Basin in Rio de Janeiro that lasted nearly five decades and ended in 1984.
Sahitisuchus was primarily terrestrial but may have lived a semi-aquatic lifestyle to some extent.

Ruiz et al. (2026) used a digital reconstruction to restore the fractured mandible of the holotype, demonstrating its utility for identifying morphological characters significant in phylogenetic studies.
It is classified as an extinct genus of sebecid mesoeucrocodylian.
The animal belongs to the family Sebecidae.
Sahitisuchus is a sebecosuchian crocodylomorph, representing a primitive form found alongside more derived Alligatoridae in the Paleocene.
Sahitisuchus belongs to the family Sebecidae.
Sahitisuchus is classified as a reptile.
The animal lived during the late Itaboraian age of the Early Eocene, approximately 53 to 50 million years ago.
It lived in the Rio de Janeiro state in southeastern Brazil during the Paleocene.
The fossils date to the late Itaboraiense age of South America, corresponding to the mid-Late Paleocene, approximately 56.5 to 58.2 million years ago.
Sahitisuchus lived from the Thanetian to the Ypresian stages, between 59.24 and 48.07 million years ago.
